notes.headline: Dell doubles revenue to a record $54.9 billion and raises its full-year outlook to $202 billion
notes.takeaway: AI servers turned Dell into a different company: revenue up 103%, earnings per share up 287%, a record $132 billion AI backlog and full-year guidance raised by $10 billion. The shares had already fallen 11.8% on the day of the report with the rest of the AI hardware trade.
results: Revenue reached a record $54.9 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and diluted earnings per share rose 287% to $8.82 (non-GAAP $9.45). The Infrastructure Solutions Group did almost all of the work: its revenue tripled to $42.0 billion, with AI-optimised servers at $22.0 billion (up 291%), traditional servers and networking at $15.0 billion and storage at $4.9 billion. Its operating income rose 308% to $7.1 billion.

The PC business barely moved: Client Solutions revenue rose 3% to $12.9 billion and operating income fell 6% to $704 million. Cash flow from operations was a record $4.5 billion in the quarter and $10.8 billion so far this year, and Dell returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders, with the board adding $25 billion to the buyback authorisation.
mgmt: Chief operating officer Jeff Clarke said Dell is “now a different company”, with the infrastructure group driving most of its profit and growth. The company booked $60.2 billion of AI orders in the quarter and ended it with a record $132.3 billion AI backlog, which he said is vetted for customers’ access to capital, land and power. More than 7,500 customers are deploying Dell AI Factories.

Dell raised full-year revenue guidance to $202 billion (from $192 billion), AI server revenue to $78 billion (from $74 billion) and non-GAAP earnings per share to $29.68 (from $25.50). For the fourth quarter it expects revenue of $56.3 billion, up 69%, and non-GAAP earnings per share of $8.40. Chief financial officer David Kennedy pointed out that non-GAAP operating expenses fell to 7% of revenue, the lowest in the company’s 42-year history.
view: These are extraordinary numbers for a company that was a slow-growing PC and server maker two years ago. The concern in the market is not demand, which the backlog makes plain, but what AI servers earn: they carry far lower gross margins than storage or traditional servers, and much of the value goes to Nvidia’s chips. Dell’s answer is scale and cost control, and the 7% operating expense ratio shows it is working: earnings are growing faster than revenue.

The shares fell 11.8% to $295.28 on the day of the report, before the results came out, as AI hardware stocks gave back the previous day’s rally and HPE dropped after its own report. At that price Dell trades at about 12 times trailing earnings and roughly 10 times its new full-year earnings guidance, a multiple that assumes this level of profit will not last.

That is the real debate. If AI infrastructure spending keeps growing into 2027–2028, Dell’s backlog and buybacks make the shares cheap. If spending pauses, server revenue can fall quickly and the PC business, which is flat, offers little cushion. I think the backlog gives unusual visibility for the next several quarters, but this is a cyclical business at a cyclical peak, and the market is right to pay a low multiple for it.
notes.watch: Whether AI orders keep exceeding shipments (backlog growth), gross margin in the infrastructure group, and any sign of order cancellations.
